tweets.text:
If you think this is a bad year for China, wait until next year:

"China has reduced the total number of banks by nearly a quarter as part of a drive to strengthen oversight of smaller lenders at a time of slower economic momentum. Regional consolidation within China’s vast state-controlled banking system, with some $64tn in overall assets, comes amid signs of sluggish demand for credit in the world’s second-largest economy. There were more than 670 closures of banking entities last year — a record high — according to official data from the National Financial Regulatory Administration. Almost all were in rural areas. The closures mean the number of entities has fallen to 3,139, down 23 per cent in the four years to 2025, the rating agency Fitch said in a report based on NFRA data. Low rates and deflation in China have also put pressure on bank profits in the shadow of a prolonged property slowdown."

Came across this post about how the GTM stack is evolving, and (I hate to admit it) it’s the first time I’m hearing about some tools in the 2025–2026 stack.

Fixing that.
Sharing here in case you’re in the same spot ↓

• @claudeai Code – the one we all know; easy
• @clay – CRM app focused on filtering lead signals
• @InstantlyAI – automated cold email platform for high-volume outreach
• @heyreach_io – LinkedIn automation platform
• @useapolloio – B2B lead database
• freckle(.io) – a simpler, more accessible alternative to Clay
• @joinergo – an automated CRM assistant that listens to calls, emails, etc.
• nooks(.ai) – AI-powered parallel dialer and virtual sales floor
• mutiny (mutinyhq(.com)) – customer-facing personalization (e.g., sales data rooms)

Lots of good tools here, but I’m curious: which ones are you using these days?

Shout out to our friends over at @greenfield_cap for this. I've known them for years, and they're one of the few VCs out there who genuinely care and actually work for their portcos.

That's why this initiative is even more meaningful to me, and the perfect example of probably many cases we could make.

We're right in the middle of a transition. A transition from a premature space full of idealistic and nice little experiments, to a grown up industry with a serious shot at disrupting the entire financial system, with the full attention of the most powerful people and institutions in the world.

But it's us that represent and build the industry. So whether this transition succeeds in the end comes down to whether we evolve and grow up too. This new era is the endgame of everything we've always wished for, but it also means the game gets tougher and more competitive than ever.

It's time we replace the lazy, delusional teams that just happened to be in the right place at the right time and lost all their hunger to overfunding, with the actual chads who want to execute and get shit done. That's what this industry deserves after all these years.

Everyone wants to enjoy the golden age of onchain businesses and mainstream adoption. Time to put the reins in the hands of the right people, and nothing stands in its way.

tweets.text:
watching AI maxis today is like watching blockchain maxis in 2021. everyone knew what blockchains were, and they were sharing similar graphs - how 0.1% of the world was using blockchains

guess what, blockchains didn't become the rails for property nfts, taxes, or identification. it is one thing to take that chart in isolation, but another to take it in conjunction w the fact that *the whole world* knows about AI. it isn't some niche thing

so if the whole world knows about something, why are so little people using it? precisely becaus they don't deem it valuable enough to pay for it. it's not that they aren't using it - the free version is just good enough. it's like google search!

modern AI debate is basically a two-camp debate between frontier gurus who are trying to build machine god (IQ 200 -> IQ 1000 jump) who are out of touch w reality and convinced no one uses AI 

vs people at the ground, seeing adoption, and realising that people don't need that - real adoption is in Muse (see # of downloads vs Chat gpt on launch) ; and that we don't need as much compute as we think we do 

and even the people on the ground are having a hard time figuring out the good biz model for AI - because again, 99% of the tasks like answering emails, booking flights are menial and not recurring enough

you know what AI is used the most for? video. i'm 100% sure vid gen will be the most successful AI vertical to ever exist (i still don't have a good long for that) 

and i think that people will converge to the reality that AI is just a useful tool, and not something groundbreaking for 90% of workplace. for the 10% (phd, academic, research, etc.) they can continue using frontier models. but 90% of consultancies, businesses, etc. will just use normal AI. and costs for that will go down so much.

tweets.text:
I’m 32 and I remember teachers telling us Wikipedia was not reliable enough to use because you couldn’t really verify who had written it, I remember my mom telling me to never ever put my credit card number online because obviously someone was going to steal it, and in Paris for a while even tapping your card to pay felt like some insecure weird thing, and then paying with your phone felt even crazier.

I also remember at school, and even later in college, there were assignments where using a computer and Word was somehow seen as cheating or lazy and you were supposed to write everything by hand.

All of these things took years to become normal, and there were always people resisting them, sometimes because they were scared of something new, and sometimes for actually pretty good reasons because the technology genuinely wasn’t that reliable yet.

I think that’s basically where we are with AI today. The person saying “there is no way I’m connecting my email to a chatbot,” or “I’m never sending an email written by AI,” or “why would I let an agent book a flight, check me in, reserve a restaurant or do random grunt work for me” sounds completely reasonable right now.

But I suspect in 10 years it will sound a lot like saying you would never put your credit card number on the internet.

These transitions always feel weird while you’re living through them. Then one day they’re just normal.

I’m 32 and I remember teachers telling us Wikipedia was not reliable enough to use because you couldn’t really verify who had written it, I remember my mom telling me to never ever put my credit card number online because obviously someone was going to steal it, and in Paris for a while even tapping your card to pay felt like some insecure weird thing, and then paying with your phone felt even crazier.

I also remember at school, and even later in college, there were assignments where using a computer and Word was somehow seen as cheating or lazy and you were supposed to write everything by hand.

All of these things took years to become normal, and there were always people resisting them, sometimes because they were scared of something new, and sometimes for actually pretty good reasons because the technology genuinely wasn’t that reliable yet.

I think that’s basically where we are with AI today. The person saying “there is no way I’m connecting my email to a chatbot,” or “I’m never sending an email written by AI,” or “why would I let an agent book a flight, check me in, reserve a restaurant or do random grunt work for me” sounds completely reasonable right now.

But I suspect in 10 years it will sound a lot like saying you would never put your credit card number on the internet.

These transitions always feel weird while you’re living through them. Then one day they’re just normal.
